claim: Yeast mother cells form a protein aggregate during early replicative aging that is maintained as a single, asymmetrically inherited deposit over the remaining lifespan.
source: In this study, we show that yeast mother cells form a protein aggregate during early replicative aging that is maintained as a single, asymmetrically inherited deposit over the remaining lifespan.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including microscopy images and quantification showing deposit formation and inheritance patterns.

claim: Deposit formation was not associated with stress or general decline in proteostasis.
source: Surprisingly, deposit formation was not associated with stress or general decline in proteostasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that deposit-containing cells maintain protein quality control functions.

claim: Deposit-containing cells displayed enhanced degradation of cytosolic proteasome substrates.
source: Rather, the deposit-containing cells displayed enhanced degradation of cytosolic proteasome substrates and unimpaired clearance of stress-induced protein aggregates.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from auxin-inducible degron assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: Deposit-containing cells showed unimpaired clearance of stress-induced protein aggregates.
source: Rather, the deposit-containing cells displayed enhanced degradation of cytosolic proteasome substrates and unimpaired clearance of stress-induced protein aggregates.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Q-body clearance times in Figure 4.

claim: Deposit formation was dependent on Hsp42.
source: Deposit formation was dependent on Hsp42, which collected non-random client proteins of the Hsp104/Hsp70-refolding machinery, including the prion Sup35.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that deletion of HSP42 abolished age-associated protein deposit formation.

claim: Hsp42 collected non-random client proteins of the Hsp104/Hsp70-refolding machinery, including the prion Sup35.
source: Deposit formation was dependent on Hsp42, which collected non-random client proteins of the Hsp104/Hsp70-refolding machinery, including the prion Sup35.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Sup35 accumulation in deposits and the role of Hsp42 in deposit formation.

claim: Loss of Hsp42 resulted in symmetric inheritance of its constituents.
source: Importantly, loss of Hsp42 resulted in symmetric inheritance of its constituents and prolonged the lifespan of the mother cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing aggregate distribution in buds of hsp42Δ mutants.

claim: Loss of Hsp42 prolonged the lifespan of the mother cell.
source: Importantly, loss of Hsp42 resulted in symmetric inheritance of its constituents and prolonged the lifespan of the mother cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by replicative lifespan data showing hsp42Δ mutants lived 39 generations compared to 27 for wild-type.

claim: Protein aggregation is an early aging-associated differentiation event in yeast.
source: Together, these data suggest that protein aggregation is an early aging-associated differentiation event in yeast, having a two-faceted role in organismal fitness.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing early deposit formation and its effects on aging.

claim: Protein aggregation has a two-faceted role in organismal fitness.
source: Together, these data suggest that protein aggregation is an early aging-associated differentiation event in yeast, having a two-faceted role in organismal fitness.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing both beneficial effects (enhanced UPS function) and detrimental effects (shortened lifespan) of the deposit pathway.

claim: Aging results in an increasing decline of the organism's fitness over time.
source: Aging results in an increasing decline of the organism's fitness over time (Lopez-Otin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lopez-Otin et al., 2013.

claim: The aging process segregates asymmetrically during budding yeast division, with the mother cell forming an aging lineage and daughters rejuvenating to form eternal lineages.
source: Remarkably, this process segregates asymmetrically during budding yeast division: the mother cell forms an aging lineage, whereas the daughters generated by these mothers rejuvenate to form eternal lineages, similar to the segregation of soma and germ lineages in metazoans.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about yeast aging and is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Lineage separation in yeast requires asymmetric inheritance of aging factors during cell division.
source: Such lineage separation requires that the inheritance of factors that promote aging, such as defective/deleterious organelles, proteins, and DNA, is asymmetric during cell division (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007; Henderson and Gottschling, 2008; Shcheprova et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2011; Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Higuchi et al., 2013; Clay et al., 2014; Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014; Henderson et al., 2014; Higuchi-Sanabria et al., 2014; Thayer et al., 2014; Katajisto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Protein aggregates and/or damaged proteins are a hallmark in the etiology of many human disorders associated with aging.
source: Protein aggregates and/or damaged proteins are a hallmark in the etiology of many human disorders associated with aging (Hartl et al., 2011; Wolff et al., 2014), and their presence correlates with aging of mitotically active yeast and drosophila stem cells (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007; Bufalino et al., 2013; Coelho et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hartl et al., 2011 and Wolff et al., 2014.

claim: The presence of protein aggregates correlates with aging of mitotically active yeast and drosophila stem cells.
source: Protein aggregates and/or damaged proteins are a hallmark in the etiology of many human disorders associated with aging (Hartl et al., 2011; Wolff et al., 2014), and their presence correlates with aging of mitotically active yeast and drosophila stem cells (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007; Bufalino et al., 2013; Coelho et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007; Bufalino et al., 2013; Coelho et al., 2013.

claim: Hsp104-mediated protein disaggregation is required for full replicative life span.
source: Studies on budding yeast have shown a correlation between the accumulation of protein aggregates and replicative aging by demonstrating that Hsp104-mediated protein disaggregation is required for full replicative life span (Erjavec et al., 2007), and that over-expression of Mca1, which counteracts the formation of stress- and age-associated protein aggregates (Lee et al., 2010; Hill et al., 2014), extends the life span of yeast mother cells (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Erjavec et al., 2007.

claim: Over-expression of Mca1 extends the life span of yeast mother cells.
source: Studies on budding yeast have shown a correlation between the accumulation of protein aggregates and replicative aging by demonstrating that Hsp104-mediated protein disaggregation is required for full replicative life span (Erjavec et al., 2007), and that over-expression of Mca1, which counteracts the formation of stress- and age-associated protein aggregates (Lee et al., 2010; Hill et al., 2014), extends the life span of yeast mother cells (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hill et al., 2014.

claim: Mca1 counteracts the formation of stress- and age-associated protein aggregates.
source: Studies on budding yeast have shown a correlation between the accumulation of protein aggregates and replicative aging by demonstrating that Hsp104-mediated protein disaggregation is required for full replicative life span (Erjavec et al., 2007), and that over-expression of Mca1, which counteracts the formation of stress- and age-associated protein aggregates (Lee et al., 2010; Hill et al., 2014), extends the life span of yeast mother cells (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2010 and Hill et al., 2014.

claim: More than 80% of cells that had undergone more than 6 divisions displayed an Hsp104-labeled aggregate.
source: Interestingly, we found many cells displaying an aggregate (typically a single bright Hsp104-labeled focus) and this portion increased in a progressive, age-dependent manner such that >80% of cells that had undergone more than 6 divisions displayed such a structure (Figure 1A,B), as previously reported (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B and citations to previous work.

claim: Hsp70 proteins Ssa1 and Ssa2 readily localized to age-associated protein deposits.
source: Co-localization analysis with Hsp104 demonstrated that the Hsp70 proteins Ssa1 and Ssa2, the small heat shock protein Hsp42, and the Hsp40 protein Ydj1 readily localized to these aggregates, the Hsp26 was found to be enriched in only 15% of Hsp104-labeled foci, while no accumulation of Hsp40 protein Sis1 or the Hsp90 protein Hsp82 was detected (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The small heat shock protein Hsp42 readily localized to age-associated protein deposits.
source: Co-localization analysis with Hsp104 demonstrated that the Hsp70 proteins Ssa1 and Ssa2, the small heat shock protein Hsp42, and the Hsp40 protein Ydj1 readily localized to these aggregates, the Hsp26 was found to be enriched in only 15% of Hsp104-labeled foci, while no accumulation of Hsp40 protein Sis1 or the Hsp90 protein Hsp82 was detected (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The Hsp40 protein Ydj1 readily localized to age-associated protein deposits.
source: Co-localization analysis with Hsp104 demonstrated that the Hsp70 proteins Ssa1 and Ssa2, the small heat shock protein Hsp42, and the Hsp40 protein Ydj1 readily localized to these aggregates, the Hsp26 was found to be enriched in only 15% of Hsp104-labeled foci, while no accumulation of Hsp40 protein Sis1 or the Hsp90 protein Hsp82 was detected (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Hsp26 was found to be enriched in only 15% of Hsp104-labeled foci.
source: Co-localization analysis with Hsp104 demonstrated that the Hsp70 proteins Ssa1 and Ssa2, the small heat shock protein Hsp42, and the Hsp40 protein Ydj1 readily localized to these aggregates, the Hsp26 was found to be enriched in only 15% of Hsp104-labeled foci, while no accumulation of Hsp40 protein Sis1 or the Hsp90 protein Hsp82 was detected (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative co-localization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No accumulation of Hsp40 protein Sis1 was detected at age-associated protein deposits.
source: Co-localization analysis with Hsp104 demonstrated that the Hsp70 proteins Ssa1 and Ssa2, the small heat shock protein Hsp42, and the Hsp40 protein Ydj1 readily localized to these aggregates, the Hsp26 was found to be enriched in only 15% of Hsp104-labeled foci, while no accumulation of Hsp40 protein Sis1 or the Hsp90 protein Hsp82 was detected (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: No accumulation of Hsp90 protein Hsp82 was detected at age-associated protein deposits.
source: Co-localization analysis with Hsp104 demonstrated that the Hsp70 proteins Ssa1 and Ssa2, the small heat shock protein Hsp42, and the Hsp40 protein Ydj1 readily localized to these aggregates, the Hsp26 was found to be enriched in only 15% of Hsp104-labeled foci, while no accumulation of Hsp40 protein Sis1 or the Hsp90 protein Hsp82 was detected (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Age-dependent appearance of protein deposits was detected in diploid cells.
source: Importantly, age-dependent appearance of these structures was also detected in diploid cells, in other strain backgrounds (W303), independently of the MEP procedure, and when different fluorophores where used for tagging Hsp104 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–H), indicating that their formation represents a general, age-dependent phenomenon of budding yeast cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–H.

claim: Age-dependent appearance of protein deposits was detected in W303 strain background.
source: Importantly, age-dependent appearance of these structures was also detected in diploid cells, in other strain backgrounds (W303), independently of the MEP procedure, and when different fluorophores where used for tagging Hsp104 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–H), indicating that their formation represents a general, age-dependent phenomenon of budding yeast cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–H.

claim: Age-dependent appearance of protein deposits was detected independently of the MEP procedure.
source: Importantly, age-dependent appearance of these structures was also detected in diploid cells, in other strain backgrounds (W303), independently of the MEP procedure, and when different fluorophores where used for tagging Hsp104 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–H), indicating that their formation represents a general, age-dependent phenomenon of budding yeast cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–H.

claim: Age-dependent appearance of protein deposits was detected when different fluorophores were used for tagging Hsp104.
source: Importantly, age-dependent appearance of these structures was also detected in diploid cells, in other strain backgrounds (W303), independently of the MEP procedure, and when different fluorophores where used for tagging Hsp104 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–H), indicating that their formation represents a general, age-dependent phenomenon of budding yeast cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–H.

claim: Most mother cells started to form the age-associated protein deposit after budding three to four times.
source: This showed that most mother cells started to form this aggregate already after budding three to four times (Figure 1D, 390 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The fastest growth phase of the age-associated protein deposit took place during the first half an hour following its detection.
source: The fastest growth phase of the aggregate took place during the first half an hour following its detection, after which the Hsp104 signal intensity increased only marginally (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of deposit growth shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Age-associated protein deposits initially underwent occasional dissolution but became stable within a few hours from nucleation.
source: While the aggregates initially underwent occasional dissolution, they became stable within a few hours from nucleation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Age-associated protein deposits faithfully segregated to the aging mother cell in 98% of divisions, irrespective of its age.
source: Pedigree analysis of aggregate inheritance in cells of different age showed that they faithfully segregated to the aging mother cell (98% of divisions), irrespective of its age (Figure 1D,F, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative pedigree analysis shown in Figure 1D,F and Video 1.

claim: Cells preferentially displayed only a single Hsp104 focus more than 80% of the time after deposit formation.
source: These cells preferentially (>80% of time) displayed only a single Hsp104 focus (Figure 1G–H), which was very stable, typically persisting until the last divisions of the cell (Figure 1G,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cells tracked in microfluidic devices shown in Figure 1G–H.

claim: The age-associated protein deposit was very stable, typically persisting until the last divisions of the cell.
source: These cells preferentially (>80% of time) displayed only a single Hsp104 focus (Figure 1G–H), which was very stable, typically persisting until the last divisions of the cell (Figure 1G,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by long-term tracking data shown in Figure 1G,I.

claim: The age-associated protein deposit displayed limited exchange of Hsp104 with the cytoplasm, with 59% of Hsp104 being immobile.
source: Moreover, this structure was largely non-dynamic, displaying limited exchange of Hsp104 with the cytoplasm, as determined by fluorescent recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) analysis in diploid cells that expressed one GFP- and one mCherry-tagged copy of HSP104 (Figure 1J). We bleached and measured the recovery of the mCherry signal (Figure 1J) and by fitting nine recovery curves, found that on average a large fraction (59%) of Hsp104 was immobile, while the mobile fraction displayed a half-time recovery rate of 8.9 s (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP analysis data shown in Figure 1J,K.

claim: The mobile fraction of Hsp104 at the age-associated protein deposit displayed a half-time recovery rate of 8.9 s.
source: We bleached and measured the recovery of the mCherry signal (Figure 1J) and by fitting nine recovery curves, found that on average a large fraction (59%) of Hsp104 was immobile, while the mobile fraction displayed a half-time recovery rate of 8.9 s (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP analysis data shown in Figure 1J,K.

claim: Sup35-GFP clearly accumulated into Hsp104-mCherry-labeled age-associated protein deposit in 33% of [PSI+] cells that contained such a deposit.
source: Importantly, Sup35-GFP clearly accumulated into Hsp104-mCherry-labeled age-associated protein deposit in 33% of [PSI+] cells that contained such a deposit, whereas no accumulation was detected in the non-prion [psi−] cells (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: No accumulation of Sup35-GFP was detected in age-associated protein deposits in non-prion [psi−] cells.
source: Importantly, Sup35-GFP clearly accumulated into Hsp104-mCherry-labeled age-associated protein deposit in 33% of [PSI+] cells that contained such a deposit, whereas no accumulation was detected in the non-prion [psi−] cells (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: The formation of bright Sup35 foci was age-dependent.
source: As expected, the formation of this bright Sup35 focus was age-dependent (Figure 2D), in line with earlier observations (Derdowski et al., 2010), but interestingly the [PSI+] state did not have an overall effect on Hsp104-labeled deposit formation (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Derdowski et al., 2010.

claim: The [PSI+] state did not have an overall effect on Hsp104-labeled deposit formation.
source: As expected, the formation of this bright Sup35 focus was age-dependent (Figure 2D), in line with earlier observations (Derdowski et al., 2010), but interestingly the [PSI+] state did not have an overall effect on Hsp104-labeled deposit formation (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Sup35 was recruited into the pre-existing age-associated protein deposit marked by Hsp104-mCherry.
source: Notably, time-lapse imaging showed that Sup35 was recruited into the pre-existing age-associated protein deposit (marked by Hsp104-mCherry).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Sup35-enriched age-associated protein deposits segregated asymmetrically towards the aging mother cell in 98% of mitoses.
source: These Sup35-enriched age-associated protein deposits segregated asymmetrically towards the aging mother cell in 98% of mitoses (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of mitotic segregation shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: Dcp2 did not accumulate into the age-associated deposit.
source: In contrast, Dcp2, a Q/N-rich component of the reversible P-body mRNP aggregates (Reijns et al., 2008), did not accumulate into the age-associated deposit (Figure 2H,I), even after induction of P-body formation by reducing the glucose level in the medium to 0.1% (Decker et al., 2007) (0/57 Hsp104 foci with Dcp2-GFP, Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2H,I,J and citations.

claim: Age-associated protein deposits and P-bodies never fused with each other.
source: Furthermore, we never observed age-associated protein deposits and P-bodies fusing with each other (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Q-bodies induced upon heat stress were transient and readily solubilized after the removal of the stress factor.
source: In stark contrast to the age-associated aggregates (Figure 1G,I), Q-bodies induced upon heat stress (42°C, 30 min) were transient and readily solubilized after the removal of the stress factor (Figure 3A; Liu et al., 2010; Escusa-Toret et al., 2013; Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A and citations.

claim: All markers of the age-associated protein deposit were found to accumulate in Q-bodies.
source: Comparative analysis of the localization of different chaperone proteins between Q-bodies and the age-associated protein deposit showed that all markers of the age-associated protein deposit were also found to accumulate in Q-bodies (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Hsp82 and Btn2 localize to Q-bodies but are excluded from the age-dependent protein deposit.
source: Conversely, we found chaperones such as Hsp82 and Btn2 localizing to Q-bodies (Figure 3B) albeit being excluded from the age-dependent protein deposit (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 1C.

claim: VHL typically formed a single focus, which in 87% of the cases did not accumulate Hsp104-mCherry within 30 min after its appearance.
source: VHL typically formed a single focus, which in 87% of the cases did not accumulate Hsp104-mCherry within 30 min after its appearance (Figure 3C,D, N = 29).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: In 98.6% of cases, Btn2 did not localize to the age-associated Hsp104-foci.
source: This analysis showed that in 98.6% of the cases, Btn2 did not localize to the age-associated Hsp104-foci (Figure 1C and Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative co-localization data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 3F.

claim: From all thirty identified cells displaying endogenous Btn2 foci, only one case showed Hsp104 enrichment at this site.
source: Moreover, from all thirty identified cells displaying endogenous Btn2 foci, we found only one case in which Hsp104 was enriched at this site (Figure 3G, N = 1268 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: More than 98% of Rnq1-foci displayed accumulation of Hsp104 within 30 min after their appearance.
source: This showed that the IPOD typically appeared as a single focus to which Hsp104 rapidly accumulated (Figure 3H,I) (>98% of Rnq1-foci displayed accumulation of Hsp104 within 30 min after their appearance, N = 53).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3H,I.

claim: Aggregating Rnq1-GFP did not accumulate to the age-associated deposit but formed a new aggregate.
source: However, by dissecting the Rnq1-GFP appearance dynamics in cell with a pre-existing age-associated protein deposit (marked by Hsp104-mCherry), we found that the aggregating Rnq1-GFP did not accumulate to the age-associated deposit (see white arrowhead in Figure 3H), but rather it formed a new aggregate to which Hsp104 then strongly accumulated, while its intensity at the age-associated protein deposit declined (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In 98.3% of [PIN+, PSI+] cells with Hsp104 foci, Rnq1-GFP did not accumulate to the age-associated deposit.
source: We analyzed altogether 117 Hsp104 foci-containing [PIN+, PSI+] cells and found that in 98.3% of the cases, Rnq1-GFP did not accumulate to this deposit (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: No difference in the mean time of protein aggregate clearance was detected between young and aged cells following acute heat stress.
source: Surprisingly, no difference in the mean time of protein aggregate clearance was detected between these populations: young: 71 ±5 min old: 72 ±4 min, n.s.) (Figure 4C), suggesting that aged cells, despite having a protein deposit, are fit to cope with proteotoxic stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Q-body clearance times shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cells with and without a pre-existing age-associated deposit showed a comparable Q-body response when heat was applied.
source: The duration of the Q-body response (state in which cells display two or more Hsp104-foci) was plotted over time and demonstrated that cells with and without a pre-existing age-associated deposit showed a comparable Q-body response when heat was applied, while cells that were not exposed to heat did not show similar Q-body response during this time period (Figure 4E, N = 53–97 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mild exposure to proteotoxic stress conditions counteracts the formation of age-associated protein deposits.
source: Surprisingly, when the cells without a prior aggregate encountered heat stress (i.e. conditions that induce proteotoxic stress), a substantially smaller portion of them (36.4%) displayed an aggregate at the end of the experiment (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The decay rate of AID-GFP was significantly accelerated in cells with an age-associated deposit when compared to neighboring cells without an Hsp104-focus.
source: Importantly, this showed that the decay rate of AID-GFP was significantly accelerated in cells with an age-associated deposit when compared to neighboring cells that did not contain an Hsp104-focus (Figure 5C,D) (rate constant (K): 0.155 ± 0.007 (with) vs 0.129 ± 0.006 (without), p < 0.01, N = 91 cells/category).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of AID-GFP degradation rates shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: No difference was detected in the decay rate of nuclear GFP between cells with or without an age-associated protein deposit.
source: However, no difference was detected in the decay rate of nuclear GFP between cells with or without an age-associated protein deposit (Figure 5E,F) (K: 0.075 ± 0.004 (with) vs 0.079 ± 0.005 (without), n.s.), demonstrating that the effect of the age-associated protein deposit on the UPS function is specific to the cytosolic compartment.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of NLS-AID-GFP degradation rates shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The effect of the age-associated protein deposit on the UPS function is specific to the cytosolic compartment.
source: However, no difference was detected in the decay rate of nuclear GFP between cells with or without an age-associated protein deposit (Figure 5E,F) (K: 0.075 ± 0.004 (with) vs 0.079 ± 0.005 (without), n.s.), demonstrating that the effect of the age-associated protein deposit on the UPS function is specific to the cytosolic compartment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential effects on cytosolic vs nuclear UPS substrates shown in Figure 5.

claim: In 24 out of 25 cells, Hsp42 was at the age-associated protein deposit before Hsp104.
source: Time-lapse microscopy showed that in 24 out of 25 cells, Hsp42 was at the age-associated protein deposit before Hsp104 and was the first protein we find to mark this structure (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Hsp42 was the first protein found to mark the age-associated protein deposit structure.
source: Time-lapse microscopy showed that in 24 out of 25 cells, Hsp42 was at the age-associated protein deposit before Hsp104 and was the first protein we find to mark this structure (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ssa1 and Hsp104 were recruited to the age-associated deposit subsequently, appearing concurrently up to 120 min after appearance of the Hsp42-focus.
source: Ssa1 and Hsp104 were recruited subsequently, appearing concurrently up to 120 min after appearance of the Hsp42-focus (Figure 6A and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Loss of the Hsp70 proteins Ssa1 and Ssa2 resulted in rapid formation of the Hsp104 focus.
source: Interestingly, loss of the Hsp70 proteins Ssa1 and Ssa2, which act synergistically with the disaggregase Hsp104 in protein refolding (Glover and Lindquist, 1998; Kim et al., 2013), resulted in rapid formation of the Hsp104 focus (Figure 6B,C) and a similar, but milder effect was detected upon deletion of HSP26.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6B,C and citations.

claim: Deletion of HSP42 abolished age-associated protein deposit formation.
source: In stark contrast, deletion of HSP42 abolished age-associated protein deposit formation (Figure 6B,C), which parallels to its function in Q-body assembly (Specht et al., 2011; Escusa-Toret et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6B,C and citations.

claim: Over-expression of Hsp42 caused precocious nucleation of age-associated protein deposit and promoted its growth.
source: Over-expression of Hsp42 caused precocious nucleation of age-associated protein deposit and promoted its growth (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: A significantly smaller fraction of cells over-expressing Hsp104 contained an age-associated protein deposit.
source: On the contrary, a significantly smaller fraction of cells over-expressing Hsp104 contained an age-associated protein deposit and while age-associated deposits still occasionally formed, they were rapidly destabilized (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: Age-associated deposits in Hsp104 over-expressing cells were rapidly destabilized.
source: On the contrary, a significantly smaller fraction of cells over-expressing Hsp104 contained an age-associated protein deposit and while age-associated deposits still occasionally formed, they were rapidly destabilized (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: The hsp104Δ mutant cells formed the age-associated protein deposit more rapidly during aging.
source: Similarly to what we found for the deletion of SSA1 and SSA2 (Figure 6B,C), the hsp104Δ mutant cells formed the age-associated protein deposit more rapidly during aging.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data comparing deposit formation rates.

claim: The deletion of HSP42 hampered formation of the Ssa1-GFP focus.
source: Again, the deletion of HSP42 had an opposite effect, hampering formation of the Ssa1-GFP focus (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Age-associated protein deposit formation was severely impaired in the hsp104∆ hsp42∆ double-mutant cells.
source: Remarkably, age-associated protein deposit formation was severely impaired in the hsp104∆ hsp42∆ double-mutant cells. These cells were crowded with punctate Ssa1-GFP (speckles), which failed to coalesce into a single regular age-associated protein deposit (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double-mutant cells were crowded with punctate Ssa1-GFP (speckles), which failed to coalesce into a single regular age-associated protein deposit.
source: Remarkably, age-associated protein deposit formation was severely impaired in the hsp104∆ hsp42∆ double-mutant cells. These cells were crowded with punctate Ssa1-GFP (speckles), which failed to coalesce into a single regular age-associated protein deposit (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Simultaneous reintroduction of Hsp104 and Hsp42 was sufficient to clear the cytoplasm of Ssa1-GFP speckles within 5 min.
source: Importantly, simultaneous reintroduction of Hsp104 and Hsp42 was sufficient to clear the cytoplasm of Ssa1-GFP speckles already within 5 min (Figure 7E, no foci).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of the reconstitution assay shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Introducing Hsp42 alone resulted in rapid disappearance of cytoplasmic speckles with concurrent formation of a single Ssa1-GFP focus.
source: In contrast, introducing Hsp42 alone resulted in rapid disappearance of cytoplasmic speckles with concurrent formation of a single Ssa1-GFP focus (Figure 7E, one focus).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of the reconstitution assay shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Reintroduction of only Hsp104 led to slow and incomplete clearance of the Ssa-1 speckles.
source: In contrary, reintroduction of only Hsp104 led to the slow and incomplete clearance of the Ssa-1 speckles, which was a reminiscent, but a milder phenotype as that observed upon conjugating the cell with hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double-mutant partner (Figure 6E, multiple foci).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of the reconstitution assay shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Hsp42 over-expression promotes [PSI+] curing.
source: In the context of the age-associated protein deposit cargo Sup35 (Figure 2), it is interesting to note that Hsp42 over-expression promotes [PSI+] curing, while its deletion results in enhanced [PSI+] induction, further supporting its role as the depositor for the age-associated protein deposit (Duennwald et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Duennwald et al., 2012.

claim: Deletion of Hsp42 results in enhanced [PSI+] induction.
source: In the context of the age-associated protein deposit cargo Sup35 (Figure 2), it is interesting to note that Hsp42 over-expression promotes [PSI+] curing, while its deletion results in enhanced [PSI+] induction, further supporting its role as the depositor for the age-associated protein deposit (Duennwald et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Duennwald et al., 2012.

claim: The age-associated protein deposit was inherited by the aging mother cell with high fidelity (98% of divisions) in both wild-type and hsp104Δ mutant cells.
source: Examining its mitotic segregation (monitored with Ssa1-GFP) in 96 wild-type and 186 hsp104Δ mutant cell divisions demonstrated that the age-associated protein deposit was in both cases inherited by the aging mother cell with high fidelity (in 98% of divisions; data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of mitotic segregation.

claim: Ssa1-GFP foci were frequently inherited by the daughter cells when both HSP104 and HSP42 were deleted.
source: In strong contrast, Ssa1-GFP foci were frequently inherited by the daughter cells when both HSP104 and HSP42 were deleted (Figure 8A, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 8A and Video 2.

claim: More than 65% of all hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double-mutant buds displayed at least one aggregate.
source: Quantification of the percentage of buds with protein deposits demonstrated that more than 65% of all hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double-mutant buds displayed at least one aggregate, compared to less than 4% in hsp104Δ and hsp42Δ single-mutant and in wild-type cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Less than 4% of buds in hsp104Δ and hsp42Δ single-mutant and wild-type cells displayed at least one aggregate.
source: Quantification of the percentage of buds with protein deposits demonstrated that more than 65% of all hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double-mutant buds displayed at least one aggregate, compared to less than 4% in hsp104Δ and hsp42Δ single-mutant and in wild-type cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Mutant hsp104∆ cells were short-lived compared to wild-type cells (21.5 vs 27 generations).
source: In accordance to previous work (Erjavec et al., 2007), mutant hsp104∆ cells were short-lived compared to wild-type cells (21.5 vs 27 generations, p < 0.001), supporting the idea that accelerated aggregate accumulation promotes aging.
evidence: The claim is supported by replicative lifespan data and citation to Erjavec et al., 2007.

claim: Deletion of HSP42 extended the lifespan of cells by more than 40% (39 generations).
source: Further supporting this notion, deletion of HSP42 extended the lifespan of the cells by more than 40% (39 generations, p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by replicative lifespan data.

claim: The lifespan of the hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double-mutant cells was similar to that of the hsp104Δ single-mutant cells (23 vs 21.5 generations).
source: The lifespan of the hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double-mutant cells was similar to that of the hsp104Δ single-mutant cells (23 vs 21.5 generations, respectively, ns.) and significantly shorter than that of the wild-type (p < 0.01) and hsp42Δ mutant cells (p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by replicative lifespan data.

claim: The over-expression of HSP42 had no effect on the lifespan.
source: The over-expression of HSP42 had no effect on the lifespan (data not shown), suggesting that the wild-type levels of Hsp42 are sufficient to provide its maximal effects on life span, which is consistent with the appearance of the deposit early in life span in the wild-type cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (not shown) and inference.

claim: Wild-type levels of Hsp42 are sufficient to provide its maximal effects on life span.
source: The over-expression of HSP42 had no effect on the lifespan (data not shown), suggesting that the wild-type levels of Hsp42 are sufficient to provide its maximal effects on life span, which is consistent with the appearance of the deposit early in life span in the wild-type cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Hsp42 overexpression has no effect on lifespan.

claim: Stressed fission yeast cells utilize a similar Hsp16-dependent mechanism for asymmetric partitioning of misfolded proteins.
source: This might represent a common mechanism to drive asymmetric segregation of aberrant proteins in dividing cells, as stressed fission yeast cells utilize a similar Hsp16-dependent mechanism for asymmetric partitioning of misfolded proteins (Coelho et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Coelho et al., 2014.

claim: The age-associated deposit can promote spatial protein quality control.
source: On one hand, the age-associated deposit can promote spatial protein quality control (Figures 4, 5) and promote cell diversity as an asymmetrically dividing structure that may harbor protein conformation encoded epigenetic information, such as the prion fold of Sup35 (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The age-associated deposit may promote cell diversity as an asymmetrically dividing structure that may harbor protein conformation encoded epigenetic information.
source: On one hand, the age-associated deposit can promote spatial protein quality control (Figures 4, 5) and promote cell diversity as an asymmetrically dividing structure that may harbor protein conformation encoded epigenetic information, such as the prion fold of Sup35 (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from the data on Sup35 accumulation.

claim: The long-term consequences of the deposit-forming pathway appear negative for the aging lineage.
source: At the same time, the long-term consequences of this pathway appear negative for the aging lineage (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from lifespan data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: UPS function may start to decline later during the aging process.
source: It is important to note, however, that our assays were conducted with relatively young cells that had recently acquired the protein deposit, and hence it is possible that UPS function starts to decline later during the aging process, as shown previously (Andersson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on citation to Andersson et al., 2013.

claim: The decreased degradation of cytosolic UPS substrates in a polyQ disease model was found to be due to the sequestration of the Hsp40 protein Sis1.
source: The decreased degradation of cytosolic UPS substrates in a polyQ disease model was found to be due to the sequestration of the Hsp40 protein Sis1 (Park et al., 2013)—a protein that was not associated with the age-associated deposit (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Park et al., 2013 and data from Figure 1C.

claim: Sis1 was not associated with the age-associated deposit.
source: The decreased degradation of cytosolic UPS substrates in a polyQ disease model was found to be due to the sequestration of the Hsp40 protein Sis1 (Park et al., 2013)—a protein that was not associated with the age-associated deposit (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The presence of the deposit might lead to increased levels of available (substrate unbound) Sis1, thereby allowing more efficient nuclear import and degradation of cytosolic UPS substrates.
source: It is thus plausible that the presence of the deposit might, for example, lead to increased levels of available (substrate unbound) Sis1, thereby allowing more efficient nuclear import and degradation of cytosolic UPS substrates.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: There is a need to better differentiate between pathophysiological protein aggregation and 'homeostatic' protein aggregation that takes place during physiological aging.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that there is a need to better differentiate between pathophysiological protein aggregation and 'homeostatic' protein aggregation that takes place during physiological aging, of which the latter might initially help to coordinate chaperones and UPS factors involved in protein quality control.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Homeostatic protein aggregation might initially help to coordinate chaperones and UPS factors involved in protein quality control.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that there is a need to better differentiate between pathophysiological protein aggregation and 'homeostatic' protein aggregation that takes place during physiological aging, of which the latter might initially help to coordinate chaperones and UPS factors involved in protein quality control.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the data showing enhanced UPS function.

claim: The age-associated protein deposit did not clearly fill out the set criterion for any of the previously characterized cytosolic deposits, including Q-bodies, JUNQ/INQ, or IPOD.
source: Related to this, the age-associated protein deposit did not clearly fill out the set criterion for any of the previously characterized cytosolic deposits, including Q-bodies, JUNQ/INQ, or IPOD, but rather seems to exist in parallel with the JUNQ and IPOD structures (Figure 1, Figure 3)—although, for example, the chaperones regulating these deposits were often shared between these structures.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative analysis shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The age-associated protein deposit seems to exist in parallel with the JUNQ and IPOD structures.
source: Related to this, the age-associated protein deposit did not clearly fill out the set criterion for any of the previously characterized cytosolic deposits, including Q-bodies, JUNQ/INQ, or IPOD, but rather seems to exist in parallel with the JUNQ and IPOD structures (Figure 1, Figure 3)—although, for example, the chaperones regulating these deposits were often shared between these structures.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparative analysis shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Pathological aggregation processes can hijack endogenous proteostasis regulatory mechanisms, possibly underlying their harmful effects in cells.
source: This favors the notion that pathological aggregation processes (mimicked e.g., by VHL and Rnq1 over-expression) can hijack endogenous proteostasis regulatory mechanisms, possibly underlying their harmful effects in cells (Park et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and citation to Park et al., 2013.

claim: Many of the long-lived asymmetrically retained proteins that accumulate to mother cells as they age were among those localizing to the age-associated protein deposit.
source: In this aspect, it is interesting to note that many of the long-lived asymmetrically retained proteins that accumulate to mother cells as they age (Thayer et al., 2014) were among those localizing to the age-associated protein deposit (including Hsp104, Ssa1, Ssa2, and Hsp26).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with data from Thayer et al., 2014.

claim: The storage of Sup35 in the age-associated deposit rendered it to be inherited by the mother cells.
source: This storage rendered Sup35 to be inherited by the mother cells (unlike a prion, analogous to a mnemon (Caudron and Barral, 2013)) (Figure 2), which is consistent with the size-dependent transmission model of Sup35-aggregates (Derdowski et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on data from Figure 2 and citations.

claim: Aging does not enhance Sup35-dependent [PSI+] prion generation.
source: However, aging does not enhance Sup35-dependent [PSI+] prion generation (Shewmaker and Wickner, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shewmaker and Wickner, 2006.

claim: Sup35 cannot escape the age-associated deposit under normal growth conditions.
source: Together, these notions suggest that Sup35 cannot escape the age-associated deposit under normal growth conditions, perhaps owing to the rigid amyloid-like packing (Saibil et al., 2012), being consistent with the durable and non-dynamic nature of these deposits.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and citation to Saibil et al., 2012.

claim: The age-associated deposit could be, at least temporarily, disassembled by the heat shock response.
source: However, this notion may come with a caveat: we found that the age-associated deposit could be, at least temporarily, disassembled by the heat shock response (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Changes in the environment might trigger the spread of prion conformers from the age-associated deposit.
source: This suggests the captivating possibility that changes in the environment might trigger the spread from the age-associated deposit.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the heat shock data.

claim: Asymmetric inheritance of damaged proteins and protein aggregates seems to be conserved in metazoan stem cells.
source: Since asymmetric inheritance of damaged proteins and protein aggregates seems to be conserved in metazoan stem cells (Rujano et al., 2006; Bufalino et al., 2013) that are also subjected to both replicative decline and segregation of lineages, we hypothesize that similar pathways that selectively segregate protein-aggregate based fate determinants asymmetrically during cell division are likely to be conserved and may contribute to cellular lineage specification across species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rujano et al., 2006 and Bufalino et al., 2013.

claim: Similar pathways that selectively segregate protein-aggregate based fate determinants asymmetrically during cell division are likely to be conserved and may contribute to cellular lineage specification across species.
source: Since asymmetric inheritance of damaged proteins and protein aggregates seems to be conserved in metazoan stem cells (Rujano et al., 2006; Bufalino et al., 2013) that are also subjected to both replicative decline and segregation of lineages, we hypothesize that similar pathways that selectively segregate protein-aggregate based fate determinants asymmetrically during cell division are likely to be conserved and may contribute to cellular lineage specification across species.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the data and citations.
